parts.name: Serosa
parts.description: Serosa (visceral peritoneum): a simple squamous mesothelium on a thin layer of loose connective tissue carrying vessels, lymphatics and fat. Its secretions let the loops slide freely. The retroperitoneal parts of the gut (most of the duodenum, ascending and descending colon) have an adventitia instead on their posterior surface.

parts.name: Outer longitudinal muscle
parts.description: Outer longitudinal layer of the muscularis externa: smooth muscle bundles running along the gut. Contraction shortens the segment; coordinated with the circular layer by the myenteric plexus it produces peristalsis and segmentation.

parts.name: Inner circular muscle
parts.description: Inner circular layer of the muscularis externa: bundles wrapped around the gut. Contraction narrows the lumen; the layer thickens to form the pyloric, ileocaecal and internal anal sphincters. The interstitial cells of Cajal (pacemakers of the slow waves) lie at its borders.

parts.name: Myenteric (Auerbach) plexus
parts.description: Myenteric (Auerbach) plexus: ganglia and interconnecting nerve strands between the circular and longitudinal muscle layers. Part of the enteric nervous system, it controls motility (peristalsis) and is modulated by vagal and sympathetic input. Ganglion cells are absent in Hirschsprung disease and lost in achalasia and Chagas disease.

parts.name: Submucosal (Meissner) plexus
parts.description: Submucosal (Meissner) plexus: small ganglia and nerve strands in the submucosa next to the muscularis mucosae. It controls epithelial secretion, absorption and local blood flow and the muscularis mucosae. In Hirschsprung disease its ganglion cells are absent too - a suction rectal biopsy, which samples the submucosa, is diagnostic.

parts.name: Lamina propria
parts.description: Lamina propria: loose (areolar) connective tissue between the crypts, rich in IgA-secreting plasma cells, lymphocytes, macrophages, eosinophils, fenestrated capillaries and lymphatics - the diffuse part of the gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT).

parts.name: Intestinal crypts (of Lieberkühn)
parts.description: Intestinal crypts (of Lieberkühn): simple tubular glands opening between the villi and reaching down to the muscularis mucosae. They are the regenerative compartment: stem cells at the base give rise to transit-amplifying cells in the lower half, which differentiate into enterocytes, goblet cells, enteroendocrine cells (e.g. I cells making CCK, S cells making secretin, K cells making GIP) and Paneth cells. Crypt hyperplasia with villous atrophy is the lesion of coeliac disease.

parts.name: Paneth cells
parts.description: Paneth cells: pyramidal cells clustered at the crypt base, with large eosinophilic (bright red) apical granules containing lysozyme, alpha-defensins and phospholipase A2. They shape the gut microbiome and form the niche that supports the neighbouring stem cells. Mainly in the small intestine, most numerous in the ileum; abnormal in Crohn disease, and their appearance in the distal colon (Paneth cell metaplasia) is a sign of chronic colitis.

parts.name: Crypt base stem cells (Lgr5+)
parts.description: Crypt base columnar stem cells (Lgr5+): slender cells wedged between the Paneth cells at the crypt base. They divide continuously to renew the whole epithelium every 3-5 days, via transit-amplifying cells; Wnt signalling from Paneth cells and the surrounding stroma keeps them in the stem state. APC mutations that switch this Wnt signalling on permanently start most colorectal cancers.

parts.name: Representative upper Brush border (microvilli)
parts.description: Brush border (striated border): thousands of microvilli on the apical surface of each enterocyte, each with a core of actin filaments anchored in the terminal web, covered by a carbohydrate-rich glycocalyx. Together with villi and plicae it multiplies the absorptive area about 600-fold. Its membrane carries the digestive enzymes - lactase, sucrase-isomaltase, maltase, aminopeptidases and enteropeptidase (duodenum) - so it stains PAS-positive and loss of lactase causes lactose intolerance. Original simplified upper-villus context retained above the approved join.

parts.name: Villus lamina propria core
parts.description: Villus core: lamina propria in the centre of the villus, containing the central lacteal, a subepithelial capillary network, strands of smooth muscle and immune cells (plasma cells, macrophages, lymphocytes).

parts.name: Central lacteals
parts.description: Central lacteal: a blind-ended lymphatic capillary in the axis of each villus. It takes up chylomicrons (absorbed dietary fat), which are too large to enter blood capillaries, and carries them via mesenteric lymphatics and the cisterna chyli to the thoracic duct - lymph (chyle) is milky after a fatty meal. The represented basal continuations join a submucosal crop collector; their deeper caliber/layout are schematic teaching context, with an actual exterior handoff rather than an embedded blind endpoint.

parts.name: Villus capillary network
parts.description: Representative continuous subepithelial capillary loops with patent lumens. Human villus cross sections show capillary-type channels rather than large arterioles or venules in the core (human ileal EM, Chan et al., 2014). Diameter and uniform thin wall are representative teaching transfers to jejunum, not jejunal population bounds. The simplified loop pattern is a teaching selection, not a reconstruction of one patient's complete network. Smooth arterial-to-venous color follows each connected loop; color is schematic instructional flow, not measured oxygenation.

parts.name: Villus smooth muscle
parts.description: Villus smooth muscle: strands from the muscularis mucosae running up the villus core beside the lacteal. Their rhythmic contraction shortens the villus and pumps chyle out of the lacteal.

parts.name: Representative upper Goblet cells
parts.description: Goblet cells: unicellular mucous glands whose apical cup (theca) is packed with mucin granules, PAS-positive and pale in H&E, above a narrow stem with the nucleus. The mucus (mainly MUC2) lubricates and protects the epithelium. They become more numerous along the gut, from the duodenum to the colon. Original simplified upper-villus context retained above the approved join.

parts.name: Submucosal arterioles
parts.description: Joined representative parent/feeder passage through the displayed surrounding layers. Thicker basal vessel walls and route caliber are schematic teaching context, distinct from the thin capillary wall inside the villus. The parent annular lumen reaches the actual crop.

parts.name: Submucosal venules
parts.description: Joined representative parent/feeder passage through the displayed surrounding layers. Thicker basal vessel walls and route caliber are schematic teaching context, distinct from the thin capillary wall inside the villus. The parent annular lumen reaches the actual crop.

parts.name: Mucosal branches
parts.description: Joined representative parent/feeder passage through the displayed surrounding layers. Thicker basal vessel walls and route caliber are schematic teaching context, distinct from the thin capillary wall inside the villus. The parent annular lumen reaches the actual crop.

parts.name: Mucosal venous branches
parts.description: Joined representative parent/feeder passage through the displayed surrounding layers. Thicker basal vessel walls and route caliber are schematic teaching context, distinct from the thin capillary wall inside the villus. The parent annular lumen reaches the actual crop.

parts.name: Muscularis mucosae
parts.description: Muscularis mucosae: a thin layer of smooth muscle (inner circular, outer longitudinal) at the base of the mucosa. It moves the mucosa locally, independently of peristalsis. In colorectal cancer, invasion through it into the submucosa is what defines an invasive carcinoma (pT1).

parts.name: Submucosa
parts.description: Submucosa: dense irregular connective tissue with the larger vessels, lymphatics and the submucosal plexus. In the jejunum it is raised with the overlying mucosa into the plicae circulares (valves of Kerckring): permanent circular folds - they do not flatten when the gut is distended - with a submucosal core. Tallest and most closely packed in the distal duodenum and jejunum, they fade out in the ileum.
